title: Why "if you build it they won't come": five ways startups break through marketing noise
summary: Jason Cohen argues that generic tactics like A/B-tested AdWords, SEO and Twitter followers are not a marketing strategy, since every startup lists the same ones. He offers ways to stand out: radical transparency, virality built into the product, a real story, a paid-acquisition machine where cost to acquire is below lifetime revenue, and borrowed credibility from relationships.

principles.text: Tactics every startup lists (A/B tests, SEO, Twitter, blog reviews) are not a strategy; you stay invisible.
principles.quote: every new startup on Earth says exactly these things.

principles.text: Radical transparency only works if you go all the way: publish revenue, make public promises, reveal your playbook.
principles.quote: you have to *truly* bare your soul if you want to compete on the transparency front. It's not for everyone, and I'm not suggesting it ought to be, but if you're going to employ it, don't half-ass it.

principles.text: If a product is meant to be viral, build it into the core usage loop; share buttons don't make a product viral.
principles.quote: if it *is* supposed to be viral it better be encoded in the DNA of the application, not bolted on as an afterthought.

principles.text: Press and word of mouth come from a story about why anyone should care, not a description of what the product does.
principles.quote: The number one mistake founders make when trying to generate press is talking about what the company *does* rather than telling a compelling *story*.

principles.text: One well-tuned story beats piles of ad tests, though finding it can take years.
principles.quote: It took me *five years* to figure out (a) I needed a story and (b) what the story was. It's hard. But one story beats a pile of AdWords A/B tests.

principles.text: Paid acquisition works if you find a repeatable model where cost to acquire a customer is below lifetime revenue, and count all true costs.
principles.quote: The average cost of acquiring a customer is `$C` (advertising, sales, support, doing demos) and the lifetime revenue you get from that customer is `$R`, so if `C < R` you have a business.
